lessons.title: TCP delivery
lessons.summary: TCP provides an ordered byte stream between endpoints, with retransmission and flow control.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: TCP provides an ordered byte stream between endpoints, with retransmission and flow control.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Sequence numbers identify bytes and acknowledgments indicate progress. Lost segments are retransmitted; congestion control adjusts sending rate. A successful send does not prove the remote application committed a transaction.

lessons.takeaway: Sequence numbers identify bytes and acknowledgments indicate progress. Lost segments are retransmitted; congestion control adjusts sending rate. A successful send does not prove the remote application committed a transaction.

lessons.title: UDP semantics
lessons.summary: UDP sends independent datagrams without transport-level delivery or ordering guarantees.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: UDP sends independent datagrams without transport-level delivery or ordering guarantees.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Applications choose whether to add retries, ordering or congestion control. A missing reply may reflect loss, filtering or an application timeout. UDP's small transport overhead does not make reliability and capacity concerns disappear.

lessons.takeaway: Applications choose whether to add retries, ordering or congestion control. A missing reply may reflect loss, filtering or an application timeout. UDP's small transport overhead does not make reliability and capacity concerns disappear.

lessons.title: DNS records
lessons.summary: DNS stores typed records under hierarchical names, including A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: DNS stores typed records under hierarchical names, including A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Resolvers ask authoritative servers or caches for a specific record type. A CNAME points to another name rather than an IP address. Query the requested type and inspect the answer and authority sections before assuming a name is absent.

lessons.takeaway: Resolvers ask authoritative servers or caches for a specific record type. A CNAME points to another name rather than an IP address. Query the requested type and inspect the answer and authority sections before assuming a name is absent.

lessons.title: DNS caching
lessons.summary: DNS resolvers cache answers according to record TTLs and local policy.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: DNS resolvers cache answers according to record TTLs and local policy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A changed authoritative answer may coexist with older cached answers until their lifetime expires. Lower TTLs help future changes only after previously cached longer TTLs expire. Applications may also maintain their own caches.

lessons.takeaway: A changed authoritative answer may coexist with older cached answers until their lifetime expires. Lower TTLs help future changes only after previously cached longer TTLs expire. Applications may also maintain their own caches.

lessons.title: Subnets
lessons.summary: A subnet groups IP addresses sharing a network prefix and determines which destinations are considered on-link.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A subnet groups IP addresses sharing a network prefix and determines which destinations are considered on-link.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: CIDR notation expresses prefix length; more prefix bits mean fewer addresses. Hosts use routes to decide whether to reach a neighbor directly or send packets through a gateway. Address overlap can make private-network connectivity ambiguous.

lessons.takeaway: CIDR notation expresses prefix length; more prefix bits mean fewer addresses. Hosts use routes to decide whether to reach a neighbor directly or send packets through a gateway. Address overlap can make private-network connectivity ambiguous.

lessons.title: Default routes
lessons.summary: A default route is the fallback route used when no more-specific destination route matches.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A default route is the fallback route used when no more-specific destination route matches.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Routing uses longest-prefix matching before metrics among equivalent candidates. The selected route determines next hop, interface and often source address. Check the actual route to the failing destination rather than only the configured gateway.

lessons.takeaway: Routing uses longest-prefix matching before metrics among equivalent candidates. The selected route determines next hop, interface and often source address. Check the actual route to the failing destination rather than only the configured gateway.

lessons.title: ARP
lessons.summary: ARP maps an on-link IPv4 address to a link-layer address such as an Ethernet MAC address.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: ARP maps an on-link IPv4 address to a link-layer address such as an Ethernet MAC address.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A host broadcasts a request and caches the reply in its neighbor table. It resolves the gateway's MAC for off-link traffic, not the remote server's MAC. Failed or stale neighbor entries can prevent otherwise correct routing.

lessons.takeaway: A host broadcasts a request and caches the reply in its neighbor table. It resolves the gateway's MAC for off-link traffic, not the remote server's MAC. Failed or stale neighbor entries can prevent otherwise correct routing.

lessons.title: Ports
lessons.summary: A transport port identifies an application endpoint within a host's transport protocol.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A transport port identifies an application endpoint within a host's transport protocol.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: TCP and UDP have separate port spaces. Connections are distinguished by protocol and endpoint addresses/ports; ephemeral source ports let clients create many connections. A bound listener, firewall allowance and application health are separate requirements.

lessons.takeaway: TCP and UDP have separate port spaces. Connections are distinguished by protocol and endpoint addresses/ports; ephemeral source ports let clients create many connections. A bound listener, firewall allowance and application health are separate requirements.

lessons.title: TCP handshake
lessons.summary: The TCP handshake establishes connection state through SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK messages.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The TCP handshake establishes connection state through SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK messages.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A repeated SYN without a reply suggests loss, filtering or unreachable service; a reset often indicates an explicit rejection. Capturing both ends distinguishes whether requests arrive and replies return. A completed handshake does not establish HTTP or TLS success.

lessons.takeaway: A repeated SYN without a reply suggests loss, filtering or unreachable service; a reset often indicates an explicit rejection. Capturing both ends distinguishes whether requests arrive and replies return. A completed handshake does not establish HTTP or TLS success.

lessons.title: TLS identity
lessons.summary: TLS encrypts a connection and can authenticate peers using certificates and a trust chain.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: TLS encrypts a connection and can authenticate peers using certificates and a trust chain.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The client validates trust, validity dates and the requested hostname. SNI tells the server which name is requested, while hostname verification checks the certificate identity. Encryption alone is not enough if certificate verification is disabled.

lessons.takeaway: The client validates trust, validity dates and the requested hostname. SNI tells the server which name is requested, while hostname verification checks the certificate identity. Encryption alone is not enough if certificate verification is disabled.

lessons.title: HTTP status
lessons.summary: HTTP status codes classify a server's response to an application-layer request.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: HTTP status codes classify a server's response to an application-layer request.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: 2xx indicates success at the HTTP layer, 4xx usually concerns the request or authorization, and 5xx indicates a server-side failure. Proxies and backends may generate different codes. Correlate response headers, body and request IDs to locate the source.

lessons.takeaway: 2xx indicates success at the HTTP layer, 4xx usually concerns the request or authorization, and 5xx indicates a server-side failure. Proxies and backends may generate different codes. Correlate response headers, body and request IDs to locate the source.

lessons.title: NAT state
lessons.summary: Network address translation rewrites addresses or ports and often keeps connection-tracking state.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Network address translation rewrites addresses or ports and often keeps connection-tracking state.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Return packets must match a live mapping. Idle expiration or exhausted translation ports can break connections without changing application code. Compare timeout policies and connection reuse across clients, gateways and load balancers.

lessons.takeaway: Return packets must match a live mapping. Idle expiration or exhausted translation ports can break connections without changing application code. Compare timeout policies and connection reuse across clients, gateways and load balancers.

lessons.title: Firewall direction
lessons.summary: Firewall rules constrain traffic based on fields such as source, destination, protocol and connection state.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Firewall rules constrain traffic based on fields such as source, destination, protocol and connection state.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Stateful filtering usually tracks return traffic; stateless rules must allow both directions explicitly. Routing and filtering are separate checks. Evaluate the path and actual source address after translation before broadening access.

lessons.takeaway: Stateful filtering usually tracks return traffic; stateless rules must allow both directions explicitly. Routing and filtering are separate checks. Evaluate the path and actual source address after translation before broadening access.

lessons.title: MTU
lessons.summary: The maximum transmission unit limits packet size over a link.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The maximum transmission unit limits packet size over a link.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Path MTU discovery learns a usable size across links, often through ICMP feedback. Blocking that feedback can allow small requests while larger transfers stall. Overlay headers reduce effective payload capacity; avoid assuming every path supports the same MTU.

lessons.takeaway: Path MTU discovery learns a usable size across links, often through ICMP feedback. Blocking that feedback can allow small requests while larger transfers stall. Overlay headers reduce effective payload capacity; avoid assuming every path supports the same MTU.

lessons.title: Packet loss
lessons.summary: Packet loss occurs when packets are discarded in transit or at an endpoint.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Packet loss occurs when packets are discarded in transit or at an endpoint.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Loss may arise from congestion, faulty links, policing or overloaded receivers. TCP retransmissions can mask loss while increasing latency. Intermediate devices may deprioritize diagnostic replies, so a single traceroute hop's loss is not proof of end-to-end loss.

lessons.takeaway: Loss may arise from congestion, faulty links, policing or overloaded receivers. TCP retransmissions can mask loss while increasing latency. Intermediate devices may deprioritize diagnostic replies, so a single traceroute hop's loss is not proof of end-to-end loss.

lessons.title: DNS negative caching
lessons.summary: DNS caches can retain negative answers such as a name or record type not existing.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: DNS caches can retain negative answers such as a name or record type not existing.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The authoritative response supplies information used to determine the negative caching lifetime. A newly created record can remain invisible to clients using a cached negative result. Compare authoritative and recursive answers before repeatedly changing the record.

lessons.takeaway: The authoritative response supplies information used to determine the negative caching lifetime. A newly created record can remain invisible to clients using a cached negative result. Compare authoritative and recursive answers before repeatedly changing the record.

lessons.title: Keepalive
lessons.summary: Keepalive mechanisms periodically test or preserve idle connections at a chosen protocol layer.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Keepalive mechanisms periodically test or preserve idle connections at a chosen protocol layer.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: TCP keepalive, HTTP reuse and application heartbeats have different semantics. Their intervals must be considered alongside intermediaries' idle timeouts. A live socket does not prove the application is healthy or making progress.

lessons.takeaway: TCP keepalive, HTTP reuse and application heartbeats have different semantics. Their intervals must be considered alongside intermediaries' idle timeouts. A live socket does not prove the application is healthy or making progress.

lessons.title: Connection pooling
lessons.summary: A connection pool reuses established connections to reduce handshake cost and limit concurrency.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A connection pool reuses established connections to reduce handshake cost and limit concurrency.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A bounded pool can protect a dependency, but requests may wait for a free connection. Stale idle connections, leaked leases and oversized pools cause different symptoms. Measure pool wait time separately from network and server execution time.

lessons.takeaway: A bounded pool can protect a dependency, but requests may wait for a free connection. Stale idle connections, leaked leases and oversized pools cause different symptoms. Measure pool wait time separately from network and server execution time.

lessons.title: Load balancing
lessons.summary: A load balancer distributes requests or connections among backends according to policy and health.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A load balancer distributes requests or connections among backends according to policy and health.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Layer-4 balancing handles transport flows; layer-7 balancing can inspect HTTP routes and headers. Health checks need to reflect readiness without amplifying failures. Session affinity can improve locality but may cause uneven load.

lessons.takeaway: Layer-4 balancing handles transport flows; layer-7 balancing can inspect HTTP routes and headers. Health checks need to reflect readiness without amplifying failures. Session affinity can improve locality but may cause uneven load.

lessons.title: Proxy headers
lessons.summary: Forwarding headers carry information about the original request across proxies.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Forwarding headers carry information about the original request across proxies.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Headers such as Forwarded or X-Forwarded-For can preserve client address and scheme. Clients can spoof them unless a trusted proxy removes or validates incoming values. Applications should trust only the configured proxy chain.

lessons.takeaway: Headers such as Forwarded or X-Forwarded-For can preserve client address and scheme. Clients can spoof them unless a trusted proxy removes or validates incoming values. Applications should trust only the configured proxy chain.

lessons.title: Retries
lessons.summary: A retry repeats an operation after a failure or uncertain outcome.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A retry repeats an operation after a failure or uncertain outcome.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Bound retries by a deadline and use backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized overload. A timeout may occur after a server committed a write, so replay safety depends on idempotency or deduplication. Retrying at multiple layers can multiply traffic.

lessons.takeaway: Bound retries by a deadline and use backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized overload. A timeout may occur after a server committed a write, so replay safety depends on idempotency or deduplication. Retrying at multiple layers can multiply traffic.

lessons.title: Timeout budgets
lessons.summary: A timeout budget limits how long an end-to-end operation may consume across its stages.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A timeout budget limits how long an end-to-end operation may consume across its stages.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Connection, TLS, request, queue and dependency timeouts should fit within the caller's deadline. Cancel work when the deadline expires so abandoned requests do not keep consuming capacity. Longer timeouts can increase concurrent load during an outage.

lessons.takeaway: Connection, TLS, request, queue and dependency timeouts should fit within the caller's deadline. Cancel work when the deadline expires so abandoned requests do not keep consuming capacity. Longer timeouts can increase concurrent load during an outage.

lessons.title: Asymmetric routing
lessons.summary: Asymmetric routing means forward and return traffic take different paths.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Asymmetric routing means forward and return traffic take different paths.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: This can be legitimate, but stateful firewalls or reverse-path filtering may reject traffic when they cannot associate both directions. Inspect routes and captures at both ends before changing filters. The client-side route alone describes only half the conversation.

lessons.takeaway: This can be legitimate, but stateful firewalls or reverse-path filtering may reject traffic when they cannot associate both directions. Inspect routes and captures at both ends before changing filters. The client-side route alone describes only half the conversation.

lessons.title: Anycast
lessons.summary: Anycast advertises the same service address from multiple locations.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Anycast advertises the same service address from multiple locations.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Routing policy selects a reachable path; it does not directly measure application health or geographic distance. Route changes can move clients to another location. Connection state and failure withdrawal behavior must be considered for stateful services.

lessons.takeaway: Routing policy selects a reachable path; it does not directly measure application health or geographic distance. Route changes can move clients to another location. Connection state and failure withdrawal behavior must be considered for stateful services.

lessons.title: BGP policy
lessons.summary: BGP exchanges reachability information between routing domains and selects paths according to policy.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: BGP exchanges reachability information between routing domains and selects paths according to policy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Attributes and local policy influence selection rather than a simple shortest physical route. Prefix filters and route validation constrain accidental or unauthorized announcements. A valid advertised route does not guarantee a healthy application behind it.

lessons.takeaway: Attributes and local policy influence selection rather than a simple shortest physical route. Prefix filters and route validation constrain accidental or unauthorized announcements. A valid advertised route does not guarantee a healthy application behind it.

lessons.title: IPv6 neighbor discovery
lessons.summary: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 to find neighbors, routers and link information.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 to find neighbors, routers and link information.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: It replaces IPv4 ARP and supports functions including router discovery and duplicate address detection. Blocking all ICMPv6 can break normal connectivity and path MTU discovery. Link-local addressing is important for local routing communication.

lessons.takeaway: It replaces IPv4 ARP and supports functions including router discovery and duplicate address detection. Blocking all ICMPv6 can break normal connectivity and path MTU discovery. Link-local addressing is important for local routing communication.

lessons.title: TCP TIME_WAIT
lessons.summary: TIME_WAIT retains state after active TCP close so delayed segments cannot be confused with a new connection.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: TIME_WAIT retains state after active TCP close so delayed segments cannot be confused with a new connection.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Many entries can be normal with high connection churn. Investigate reuse, ephemeral-port availability and workload before changing kernel timeouts. Removing this protection indiscriminately can introduce subtle connection failures.

lessons.takeaway: Many entries can be normal with high connection churn. Investigate reuse, ephemeral-port availability and workload before changing kernel timeouts. Removing this protection indiscriminately can introduce subtle connection failures.

lessons.title: Queueing
lessons.summary: Queues buffer bursts when work arrives faster than it can immediately be processed.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Queues buffer bursts when work arrives faster than it can immediately be processed.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: As utilization approaches capacity, waiting time can grow sharply. Larger queues delay rejection but do not add service capacity. Bound queues, measure wait time and apply backpressure or shedding when deadlines can no longer be met.

lessons.takeaway: As utilization approaches capacity, waiting time can grow sharply. Larger queues delay rejection but do not add service capacity. Bound queues, measure wait time and apply backpressure or shedding when deadlines can no longer be met.

lessons.title: TLS termination
lessons.summary: TLS termination decrypts a connection at an intermediary such as a load balancer or proxy.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: TLS termination decrypts a connection at an intermediary such as a load balancer or proxy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The next hop may be plaintext or a separately authenticated encrypted connection. Termination boundaries determine certificate ownership and where sensitive data becomes visible. Document both hops; external HTTPS alone does not prove backend encryption.

lessons.takeaway: The next hop may be plaintext or a separately authenticated encrypted connection. Termination boundaries determine certificate ownership and where sensitive data becomes visible. Document both hops; external HTTPS alone does not prove backend encryption.

lessons.title: Idempotency
lessons.summary: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated as when performed once.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated as when performed once.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A server can use an idempotency key to recognize retries and return the original outcome. Keys need a defined scope, retention policy and conflict behavior. Transport reliability cannot by itself prevent duplicate business operations.

lessons.takeaway: A server can use an idempotency key to recognize retries and return the original outcome. Keys need a defined scope, retention policy and conflict behavior. Transport reliability cannot by itself prevent duplicate business operations.

commands.title: Interface addresses
commands.definition: Shows concise interface states and assigned addresses.
commands.purpose: Confirm the source interface and address before tracing a path.
commands.environment: Read-only Linux command; example values are documentation addresses.
commands.interpretation: UP is link state; address suffixes show prefix length. An address alone does not prove a usable route.
commands.safety: Read-only Linux command; example values are documentation addresses.

commands.title: Route selection
commands.definition: Asks the kernel which route it would use for one destination.
commands.purpose: Check next hop, output interface and selected source address.
commands.environment: Read-only; substitute the actual destination and consider policy routing.
commands.interpretation: via is next hop, dev is interface and src is chosen local source.
commands.safety: Read-only; substitute the actual destination and consider policy routing.

commands.title: Neighbor state
commands.environment: Read-only; use ip -6 neigh for IPv6-specific inspection.
commands.interpretation: REACHABLE is recently confirmed; STALE can be normal; FAILED indicates unsuccessful resolution.
commands.safety: Read-only; use ip -6 neigh for IPv6-specific inspection.

commands.title: DNS answer
commands.definition: Queries DNS for IPv4 address records.
commands.purpose: Inspect response code, returned records and TTLs.
commands.environment: Read-only network query; DNS results are illustrative.
commands.interpretation: status NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist in that response; ANSWER records include remaining TTL.
commands.safety: Read-only network query; DNS results are illustrative.

commands.title: Specific resolver
commands.definition: Directs a DNS query to a chosen resolver.
commands.purpose: Compare two resolvers during inconsistent resolution.
commands.environment: Replace the documentation address with an authorized resolver; a timeout does not prove the record is absent.
commands.interpretation: The SERVER field confirms the queried resolver; compare status, answer and TTL, not only the final address.
commands.safety: Replace the documentation address with an authorized resolver; a timeout does not prove the record is absent.

commands.title: DNS authority chain
commands.definition: Walks DNS delegation from root toward authoritative servers.
commands.purpose: Locate a delegation or authority discrepancy.
commands.environment: Generates multiple DNS queries; does not test every application's resolver cache.
commands.expectedOutput: NS referrals followed by an authoritative answer
commands.interpretation: Each referral identifies the next authoritative servers. Failure can also reflect blocked outbound DNS from the test host.
commands.safety: Generates multiple DNS queries; does not test every application's resolver cache.

commands.title: HTTP response
commands.definition: Requests HTTP headers using HEAD with a total time limit.
commands.purpose: Inspect status, redirects and cache headers without downloading the body.
commands.environment: Read-only request but still reaches the service; use a known safe endpoint.
commands.interpretation: The status line identifies response class; Location identifies redirect destination. Some services treat HEAD differently from GET.
commands.safety: Read-only request but still reaches the service; use a known safe endpoint.

commands.title: HTTP timing
commands.definition: Measures cumulative milestones for one HTTP request.
commands.purpose: Distinguish name resolution, connection, TLS and total duration.
commands.environment: Use an authorized read endpoint; one sample is not a latency distribution.
commands.interpretation: Times are cumulative seconds from request start; subtract adjacent milestones for stage estimates.
commands.safety: Use an authorized read endpoint; one sample is not a latency distribution.

commands.title: TLS verification
commands.definition: Connects with TLS, supplies SNI and validates certificate identity.
commands.purpose: Inspect chain, negotiated protocol and verification errors.
commands.environment: Uses the system trust configuration; never interpret disabling verification as a production fix.
commands.interpretation: Check verification result and hostname; a completed encrypted handshake without verification is insufficient.
commands.safety: Uses the system trust configuration; never interpret disabling verification as a production fix.

commands.title: TCP socket detail
commands.definition: Shows established TCP connections with internal transport information.
commands.purpose: Investigate retransmission, congestion and round-trip behavior.
commands.environment: Read-only; field availability depends on kernel and iproute2 version.
commands.interpretation: rtt estimates round-trip time; retrans fields and congestion information provide transport clues, not application health.
commands.safety: Read-only; field availability depends on kernel and iproute2 version.

commands.title: Bounded packet capture
commands.definition: Captures up to fifty matching packets on one interface.
commands.purpose: Check whether SYNs, replies and resets traverse the observed point.
commands.environment: Requires capture privileges; use a scoped filter and protect captured metadata or payloads.
commands.interpretation: S is SYN, S. is SYN-ACK, R is reset; compare direction and timing.
commands.safety: Requires capture privileges; use a scoped filter and protect captured metadata or payloads.

commands.title: Path probe
commands.definition: Probes a path with increasing hop limits, bounded to fifteen hops.
commands.purpose: Locate routing changes and broad failure boundaries.
commands.environment: Generates diagnostic traffic; confirm tool availability and authorized target.
commands.interpretation: Asterisks mean no probe reply, not necessarily forwarded traffic loss. Routers may suppress or deprioritize replies.
commands.safety: Generates diagnostic traffic; confirm tool availability and authorized target.

debugging.title: DNS differs between clients
debugging.symptom: Some clients reach an old address after a DNS change.

steps.evidence: Compare authoritative answers, recursive answers and TTLs from affected and unaffected clients. Check local hosts entries and application caches separately.
Correct an authoritative mistake if present; otherwise allow documented cache lifetimes or refresh a specific managed cache. Do not keep changing the record while valid old answers remain cached.
Confirm affected clients obtain the intended address and successful requests after the old TTL window.

references.title: DNS differs between clients — primary documentation

debugging.title: TCP connection times out
debugging.symptom: A client repeatedly sends connection attempts without receiving a response.

steps.evidence: Capture at appropriate authorized points on both ends. Determine whether SYN arrives, a SYN-ACK leaves and the return path reaches the client.
Correct the evidenced route, listener or narrow firewall rule. If replies take another path, examine stateful filtering and source selection.
Observe a completed handshake and a successful application request, not merely a passing ping.

references.title: TCP connection times out — primary documentation

debugging.title: Connection refused
debugging.symptom: A service address responds with an immediate TCP reset.

steps.evidence: Check the destination host's listener, port and bind address; confirm the client reaches the intended host. A reset suggests active rejection rather than silent packet loss.
Start or correct the intended service, fix port mapping or correct an explicit rejection policy after confirming ownership.
Connect from the original client and verify the expected application identity and response.

debugging.title: TLS hostname failure
debugging.symptom: HTTPS connects but certificate verification reports a name mismatch.

steps.evidence: Inspect the certificate names, chain and selected virtual host. Confirm DNS points to the intended endpoint and SNI uses the requested hostname.
Install the correct certificate or fix routing/SNI configuration. Keep verification enabled; bypassing it does not repair identity.
Repeat verification with the real client trust store and hostname, then test application traffic.

debugging.title: Large transfers stall
debugging.symptom: Small health checks pass but larger HTTPS responses repeatedly hang.

steps.evidence: Compare effective MTU along tunnels and inspect retransmissions and ICMP packet-too-big feedback. Distinguish a path-MTU black hole from server-side buffering.
Correct tunnel MTU or permit required ICMP feedback using the network's policy. Apply MSS adjustment only when justified by the path design.
Test representative payload sizes in both directions and confirm retransmissions and stalls disappear.

debugging.title: Idle pooled connections fail
debugging.symptom: The first request after idle time fails, while an immediate retry succeeds.

steps.evidence: Compare application pool idle lifetime with proxy, load-balancer and NAT idle timeouts. Check whether the client reuses a connection already expired by an intermediary.
Expire or validate pooled connections before the shortest relevant idle timeout and bound retry behavior for safe operations.
Repeat a controlled idle interval and confirm the first request succeeds without a retry burst.

references.title: Idle pooled connections fail — primary documentation

debugging.title: Retry-amplified outage
debugging.symptom: A dependency slows and incoming requests multiply despite steady user traffic.

steps.evidence: Compare attempt counts at each layer with original request volume and dependency saturation. Identify synchronized retries and missing overall deadlines.
Cap retries, add backoff with jitter and shed excess work. Restore dependency headroom before gradually returning normal traffic.
Confirm attempts per user request, queue age and error rate return to expected levels.

debugging.title: Wrong client address in logs
debugging.symptom: Every request appears to come from a proxy, or clients can spoof recorded IP addresses.

steps.evidence: Inspect the trusted proxy chain and how forwarding headers are stripped, added and consumed. Do not trust arbitrary incoming X-Forwarded-For values.
Configure edge proxies to sanitize headers and applications to trust only known proxy hops. Preserve the actual transport peer for audit.
Test normal and deliberately supplied forwarding headers and confirm the recorded identity follows the trusted chain.

references.title: Wrong client address in logs — primary documentation

debugging.title: Intermittent backend failures
debugging.symptom: Only some requests through a load balancer fail.

steps.evidence: Correlate failures with backend identity, zone and version. Compare health-check paths with the failing business operation and inspect session affinity.
Remove or repair the evidenced unhealthy cohort while retaining capacity. Correct health checks if they pass on broken serving paths.
Verify every intended backend passes representative requests and aggregate errors recover across zones.

debugging.title: Outbound connections exhausted
debugging.symptom: New outbound connections fail during traffic spikes while established ones continue.

steps.evidence: Compare connection churn, source-port usage and NAT allocation metrics. Many TIME_WAIT entries alone are not proof of exhaustion; confirm allocation failures.
Reuse connections appropriately, bound concurrency and expand the constrained egress capacity if justified. Avoid arbitrary TCP timeout reductions.
Load-test within approved limits and verify new connections succeed with stable port and NAT headroom.
